claims: 'Super sacrifice is the most tax-effective option for most Australian employees'
whys: A population claim ('most Australian employees') with no figure or source.
constants: none (cite a source or reword to a condition on the marginal rate)

claims: Services Australia uses ATI for Family Tax Benefit, childcare subsidies 'and other income-tested payments'
'Salary sacrifice reduces taxable income but increases those reportable items, so ATI remains similar'
whys: Income support payments such as JobSeeker use the social security ordinary income test, not adjusted taxable income. Only FTB and Child Care Subsidy clearly use ATI.

Novated-lease and other non-super benefits are added back to ATI at the grossed-up reportable fringe benefit amount, so ATI can rise rather than stay similar. The claim holds for sacrificed super only.

claims: A salary sacrifice arrangement cannot reduce cash earnings below the national minimum wage or the award/agreement rate, and the employer must reject or reduce the arrangement
whys: No legal basis is cited (Fair Work Act s 324 deductions, or the salary sacrifice clause in the National Minimum Wage Order). The rule about whether sacrificed amounts count toward the minimum is not clear-cut, so this needs checking against the FWO before it is stated as a definite rule.
constants: Needs a cited FWO source; figures come from EMPLOYMENT.minimumWageHourly/Weekly

claims: 'At a 6% mortgage rate, salary sacrifice into super typically delivers a better after-tax outcome because the concessional tax rate is lower than the marginal rate'
whys: The 6% is hardcoded and has no source. The argument compares a tax-rate gap with a mortgage rate but does not account for the expected super return. It is an opinion presented as a rule, so it needs labelled editorial judgment or a worked figure from code.

claims: 'Up to ${SECOND.max}, your marginal income tax rate is ${SECOND.rate} ... the same as the ${CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE} contributions tax'
whys: 'the same as' is fixed wording. It is true for 2026-27 (15% and 15%) but breaks if either rate changes (in 2025-26 it was 16% against 15%). It also ignores the $0 to $18,200 tax-free band.
constants: TAX_BRACKETS[1].rate vs CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE (make the comparison conditional in code)

claims: "Put 30% of your second job income into a separate savings account."
whys: The 30% is typed into the prose. No constant or source backs it, and it is advice written as a rule. It should either come from the no-TFT scale or be labelled guidance.
constants: none (could derive from withholdingForPeriod / NO_TFT_START_RATE in lib/constants/payg-withholding)

claims: "tax-free threshold of $18,200" and "the first $18,200" (also line 123 "first $18,200"; line 141 "$60,000" primary job).
whys: The figures are correct today but typed into the JSX. Line 78 uses TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD, and the table at lines 156/158 uses a separate 60000 literal, so these figures can drift.
constants: TAX_FREE_THRESHOLD in lib/constants; a shared PRIMARY_JOB constant for the 60000 table base
reviewerNotes: Valid: the answer gives the National Minimum Wage the 4.75% award increase. Per the brief's known-correct facts, the NMW rose 5.97%. The same issue is at line 88. Not changed (no new numbers).

claims: This calculator provides estimates based on current ATO PAYG withholding schedules.
whys: Job 1 and the combined figures are not withholding. They are year-end liability from calculateIncomeTax minus LITO plus calculateMedicareLevy. Only Job 2 uses the Schedule 1 withholding scale. I fixed the Job 2 sentence, which still said 'approximate rate' after the code moved to the real scale. The first sentence of this legal notice was left alone.
constants: lib/constants calculateIncomeTax / calculateLITO / calculateMedicareLevy; lib/constants/payg-withholding withholdingForPeriod
